name: Carian
confidence_why: Carian evidently had a word accent that protected one vowel while the others were reduced or lost (Simon 2023 on Egyptian loanwords, Adiego 2019 on pretonic weakening), but Simon 2025 says outright that the rules of that vowel loss still elude us and Kloekhorst 2022 calls knowledge of Carian rudimentary, so no source places the accent and the few specialists agree it is undetermined.

Is it the Carian accent mapped onto the Egyptian words, or does the placement of the accent follow the Egyptian original? Words in the group with two vowels (a vowel and an [i]) all follow the Egyptian original, and as far as it can be judged, the same applies to those in the group with one vowel, too ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Carian had a strong dynamic (stress) accent: only the accented vowel of a word survives/is written, unaccented vowels are reduced or deleted (a post-tonic [i] may remain). The position of the accent is not fixed by any stated rule: in loans it stays where the source language had it, and in native words it is recoverable only per word from which vowel is. Adiego 2019: 24 adds that pretonic syllables were weakened and tonic syllables lengthened, with the accent moving onto suffixes (*knda(acute)wa- 'king' vs. *kndawa-sa(acute) 'kingship' > kδuso). No source opened gives a positional (initial/penult/etc.) rule; the reading 'lexical' is an inference from these statements, not an explicit claim of the sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Post-tonic [i] (from Egyptian schwa) may be kept (ntokris, ptnupi, ttbazi); apmen keeps a pretonic a- as an anaptyctic vowel because initial pm- was not permitted; artmon (Greek Artemon) apparently contradicts the rule but may be a local name form; pismaśk shows secondary epenthetic i.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent inferred from spellings of personal names and loanwords (Caromemphite corpus, 7th-5th c. BC) and from Greek renderings; Carian script does not mark accent, so all statements are reconstructive. Simon's rule is synchronic loan adaptation which he extends to native 'vowelless' spellings; Hajnal 1995:17-21 proposed the same as a historical rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Carian (xcr, cari1274), an alphabetically written Anatolian corpus language (7th-3rd c. BC); the accent evidence comes chiefly from the Caromemphite (Carian-of-Egypt: Saqqara/Memphis) sub-corpus and from Greek renderings of Carian names, not from a living variety. No dialect split relevant to glottocodes.

sources.note: pp. 246-249: from Egyptian (and Greek) names/loans written in Carian, formulates the rule that Carian kept only the accented vowel and dropped/left unwritten all unaccented vowels (except a post-tonic [i]); accent placement in loans follows the source language; says this rule 'generally explains the vowellessness of the Carian words'; notes Hajnal 1995:17-21 already proposed historically that only accented vowels were preserved. No positional rule for native word accent.

sources.note: p. 24 (sec. 8.2): 'It seems that in Carian there was a tendency to weaken pretonic syllables, together with a tendency to lengthen tonic syllables (and, in the case of a-macron-acute, to round in o). Thus *knda(acute)wa- > /kndow-/, but *kndawa+sa(acute) > /kndusow-/. A comparable phenomenon can be detected in kbid- vs. kbdyns.. and perhaps also in the personal name Usseldomos/Ussaldomos vs. usol.. */usa(acute)lla-/ > /usol/, but */usalla(acute)ma-/ > */us@lom-/.' I.e. accent position reconstructed per word/etymologically, shifting rightward under suffixation; no general placement rule.
